results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.draft_locus: Journey SLOs: Defining Reliability Where Liquidity Is Made ¶4
results.quote: counting failed and slow human requests against about 7 billion search requests in a 28-day period.
results.finding: The paragraph ends on the 30% figure and never says what it shows. The spec's evidence is there to show that one peak-hour incident can spend about a third of a month's budget, so the policy bites; the draft leaves that inference (and the arithmetic that slow requests make up most of it) to the reader. Flow reader A (item 6) stopped here to check the numbers.

results.draft_locus: Cost: Making Scale Visible per Unit of Work ¶3
results.quote: partly because its listings carry more revenue; the unit cost should be read against revenue per listing, not alone
results.finding: The reading of the Motorvane row gives higher revenue per listing as a cause of higher cost, which does not follow. The spec's reading is that Motorvane's high unit cost must be judged against its higher revenue per listing; the draft should state revenue as the yardstick, not as a cause.

The declared relationship is contrast: it carries over trade-offs that hold for every vertical and introduces where the verticals differ. 'differ too' frames the section as one more item after the trade-offs, not as a contrast with choices that hold everywhere, and it does not pick up the carried-over idea. Flow reader B also called this bridge very thin.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Forty-Eight Minutes on a Sunday Evening ¶5
results.quote: The "Sunday-evening peak" is a Veldmark illustration; the documented public example of a marketing-driven peak is Rightmove's
results.finding: Reader A (item 2): after Ingrid's question, 'which the rest of this chapter answers', the hand-off is complete, so this source note 'feels out of place and weakens the end of the scene'. Both readers propose moving it before the question or into the traffic-shape section. The spec places p09 as the scene's last paragraph, after the question, so the difficulty comes from the declared order, not the prose.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B item 1 (sourcing note after Ingrid's question dilutes the hand-off; belongs in traffic shape)

results.draft_locus: Journey SLOs: Defining Reliability Where Liquidity Is Made ¶3
results.quote: so the objective covers every surface.
results.finding: Reader A (item 5): 'The "so" was also hard to follow: I re-read the sentence to see that the bike incident is the reason the objective covers alerts and pages, not only search.' The clause order hides the point that the bike left search but not the digest; the prose should state that contrast before the conclusion.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B item 3 (the 'so' only became clear on the second pass)

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶1
results.quote: keep batch work out of peak windows with the peak calendar set out under capacity planning
results.finding: Reader A (item 7): the calendar 'is relied on twice before its own subsection explains it'. Reader B (item 4): 'set out under capacity planning' first read as an instruction, not a pointer to a later section. The forward reference is in the spec, but the wording is what made both readers stop; a clear pointer and a one-clause gloss of what the calendar holds would fix it without reordering.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B item 4 (clumsy forward reference to the calendar, re-read)

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶2
results.quote: The first control point is the edge, where automated traffic is classified, and policy for it starts from why bots come.
results.finding: Reader A (item 8): 'The sentence joins two ideas with "and", and "it" is ambiguous (the edge, or automated traffic?). I re-read it.' The order (load in traffic shape, control at the edge) is the spec's and both readers accepted it; the opening sentence is the problem.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B item 5 (three ideas packed into one sentence, ambiguous 'it', re-read)

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶6
results.quote: OLX is reported to have published a two-part post in 2021 on load shedding with NGINX using adaptive concurrency control; it could not be retrieved or verified for this book, so treat it as a pointer, not evidence.
results.finding: Reader A (item 9): 'This aside about the book's own sourcing breaks the retries and admission discussion. It is out of place in the body.' The spec lists this unretrieved OLX post as p22's evidence ('Marked as a pointer, not evidence'), so the draft cannot drop or move it without a spec change.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B item 7 (note about sources interrupts the explanation of admission control)

results.draft_locus: Cost: Making Scale Visible per Unit of Work ¶1
results.quote: In this book, **cost per search** means the fully allocated run cost
results.finding: Reader A (item 18): 'The formal definition of a slightly different term ("cost per search", not "per thousand") sits inside the first bullet of a list. It reads as an interruption.' The definition should come before the list or be stated for the same unit the bullet names.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-B item 11 ('The first bullet also defines "cost per search" inside the entry for "cost per thousand searches", which made me re-read it')

results.quote: The evidence comes from SRE, Vinted, Adevinta, Rightmove, FinOps and bot reports.
results.finding: Reader A (item 1): the roadmap's nested parentheses are dense and 'the sentence about evidence interrupts the roadmap before its last item'; A re-read it. Reader B noted the bare closing list but said it did not confuse.

results.draft_locus: Journey SLOs: Defining Reliability Where Liquidity Is Made ¶4
results.quote: The brown-out alone spent about **30%** of Tradeyard NL's 28-day search budget in 48 minutes
results.finding: Reader A (item 6): stopped to reconcile 30% with the 3.4 million failed requests; 'the reader has to do the arithmetic to see that the numbers agree'.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶4
results.quote: Behind the edge, the brown-out happened because interactive queries, reindexing and cache warm-up shared the same nodes at the same time.
results.finding: Reader B (item 6): 'Behind the edge' attaches to 'the brown-out happened', which briefly reads as if the brown-out happened behind the edge.

results.draft_locus: Multiple Regions: How Far to Go ¶1
results.quote: Losing a site is degradation's larger form.
results.finding: Reader A (item 11): 'The bridge is so compressed that I paused to see how regions relate to degradation.' Reader B found it terse but clear.

results.draft_locus: Cost: Making Scale Visible per Unit of Work ¶1
results.quote: search infrastructure cost divided by search requests
results.finding: Reader B (item 11): 'searches', 'queries' and 'search requests' drift across the capacity and cost sections (the capacity model counts queries with a 2.6 fan-out, the cost bullet divides by search requests, the table reports cost per 1,000 queries); B stopped to confirm they are the same unit.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶1
results.quote: keep batch work out of peak windows with the peak calendar set out under capacity planning
results.finding: 'Peak and campaign calendar' is on the audience's does_not_know list. It is relied on here, in the Figure 3 caption and in isolation rule 1 ('a calendar the platform enforces') before Capacity Planning ¶5 defines it. A one-clause gloss at first use would settle it. Other names both flow readers stopped at (Femke, the Rotterdam city bike, Ghost Inventory, Fast Mail for Fraudsters, Yardstick, Keybridge, Common Ground, the register of copies, the part's opening test) are on already_knows and are not failures.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-A item 7 (the calendar is relied on twice before its own subsection explains it)
